title: Remember Your Creator, and the Whole Duty of Man
summary: The Teacher urges the young to remember their Creator before the days of old age and death arrive, which he describes in a haunting poem of a house falling silent, a lamp shattered, and dust returning to the ground while the spirit returns to God. The motto of the book returns: everything is futile. Then a second voice, the frame narrator, describes the Teacher's work and gives the conclusion: fear God and keep his commandments, for God will bring every deed into judgment.
story: Chapter 11 ended by calling the young to rejoice in their youth while knowing that God will judge. Chapter 12 continues without a break, adding the book's most urgent command: remember your Creator. The poem on old age and death is the last thing the Teacher says, and the motto of verse 8 repeats the book's opening words (1:2), closing the frame around his search. Then, in verses 9 to 14, the narrator who introduced the Teacher in 1:1 steps forward to speak about him and to address the reader directly as my son. This epilogue tells us how to hear everything that came before. The book ends not with an answer to every question the Teacher raised, but with the fear of God and the certainty of his judgment.
historical: The chapter has no datable events, but its epilogue gives a glimpse of the world of ancient wisdom teachers. The Teacher is described as one who taught the people knowledge and who weighed, studied, and arranged many proverbs (verse 9), the work of a sage who collected and shaped sayings. Proverbs 25:1 describes similar work done by the men of Hezekiah, who copied out proverbs of Solomon. The mention of many books in verse 12 suggests a setting where written texts were multiplying, which some scholars take as a sign of the later Persian or Greek period, though writing and collecting were long established in the ancient Near East. As with the book's authorship, readers differ on whether the epilogue was written by the same person who composed the Teacher's words or by a later editor.
cultural:
The poem of verses 1 to 7 uses images of a great household in decline. Many readers since ancient times have read it as an allegory of the aging body: the keepers of the house who tremble are the arms and hands, the strong men who stoop are the legs, the grinders who cease because they are few are the teeth, those who look through the windows are the eyes, the doors to the street and the sound of the mill may be the ears or lips, the almond blossom is white hair, and the grasshopper that drags itself along is the stiff gait of old age. Others read the poem more literally as a picture of a household or town falling silent at a death, with mourners walking the streets (verse 5), or as a gathering storm that darkens the world. Many readers combine these, hearing both an aging body and a dying house.

Verse 6 uses images of objects that break: a silver cord holding a golden lamp bowl, a pitcher at a spring, and a wheel at a well used to draw water. Each pictures the end of life's supply. Verse 7 echoes Genesis 2:7 and 3:19, where God forms man from dust and breathes life into him, and says that the dust will return to the earth. The goads of verse 11 were pointed sticks used to drive oxen, and nails were fixed firmly: the words of the wise both prod and stabilize.
literary: The chapter has three parts. Verses 1 to 7 are one long sentence in Hebrew, hanging on the command remember and marked by the repeated word before (verses 1, 2, and 6). The poem moves from the fading of light to the silence of a house and finally to death. Verse 8 repeats the motto of 1:2 in shorter form, closing the frame that opened the book. Verses 9 to 14 are the epilogue, spoken in the third person about the Teacher, which shows that the book has been presented all along by a second voice, the frame narrator. This narrator praises the Teacher as wise and his words as upright and true, warns against endless study, and gives the conclusion. Interpreters differ on how the epilogue relates to the Teacher's words: some see it as endorsing him, others as gently correcting him, and many see it as drawing out what the Teacher's search had been driving at all along.

outline.t: Remember your Creator before the darkness
The house falls silent: old age and the approach of death
The silver cord, the golden bowl, dust and spirit
The motto returns: futility of futilities
The narrator on the Teacher and the words of the wise
The conclusion: fear God and keep his commandments

doctrines.note: God is the Creator to be remembered (12:1), the one who formed humanity from dust and gave the spirit that returns to him (12:7). To remember him is not merely to recall a fact but to live in dependence and gratitude toward the one who made you.

God will bring every deed into judgment, including every hidden thing, good or evil (12:14). The book's closing words give weight to every action. Nothing done under the sun is finally meaningless, because God will weigh it.

The words of the wise are goads and nails given by a single Shepherd (12:11). Wisdom both prods and steadies, and it has its source beyond the human teacher. The epilogue also warns that endless study wearies; wisdom's goal is the fear of God, not the accumulation of books.

The conclusion joins the fear of God with keeping his commandments (12:13). After all the Teacher's questions, the book lands on the covenant obedience taught by the law and the prophets, not as an answer that removes every mystery but as the right response to it.

words.note: Qoheleth, the Teacher. The title comes from a verb meaning to gather or assemble, so it may mean one who gathers people to teach them, or one who gathers sayings. It appears three times in this chapter (verses 8, 9, and 10), always in the narrator's voice. The epilogue's description of the Teacher weighing and arranging proverbs fits the sense of a gatherer of wisdom.

Bara, to create. In verse 1 its participle is used as a title: your Creator. This is the same verb used in Genesis 1:1, which in its basic form always has God as its subject. Some modern scholars have suggested that the Hebrew consonants also allow a play on words meaning your well or your grave, but the text as it stands says Creator, and the call to remember him frames the poem on death.

Hevel, breath or vapor, translated futility. It appears three times in verse 8, the motto that closes the Teacher's words. Readers differ on whether hevel means emptiness, brevity, or what is beyond comprehension. Whichever sense is primary, verse 8 sums up the Teacher's search, and the epilogue answers it: in a world of hevel, what remains is to fear God and keep his commandments.

Dorvan, goad. A goad was a sharpened stick used to prod oxen forward while plowing. In verse 11 the words of the wise are like goads: they sting, provoke, and move the hearer to action. The image fits Ecclesiastes itself, a book that unsettles its readers in order to drive them toward the fear of God.

christ: The Teacher asks what lasting gain a person can find in a world of hevel, and the epilogue points to the fear of God and his judgment. The New Testament takes up this question directly. Paul says that the creation was subjected to futility, using the Greek word (mataiotes) that the ancient Greek translation of Ecclesiastes uses for hevel, and that it will be set free from its bondage to decay into the freedom of the glory of the children of God (Romans 8:20-21). Christ's resurrection is the ground of that hope, and it is why Paul can tell believers that their labor in the Lord is not in vain (1 Corinthians 15:58). The single Shepherd who gives the words of the wise (12:11) is most naturally God himself; Jesus later calls himself the good shepherd (John 10:11), a connection of theme rather than prediction. And the final judgment of every deed is, according to the New Testament, the judgment of Christ (2 Corinthians 5:10), the one who also bore judgment for his people.

hard.q: Does the epilogue contradict the Teacher, or was it added to make a skeptical book acceptable?
hard.a: Some scholars have argued that the epilogue was added by a later editor to soften a skeptical book and secure its place among the sacred writings. Others, including the scholar Michael V. Fox, have argued that the book was designed from the start as the words of the Teacher framed by a narrator, so that the epilogue belongs to its structure. Among those who see a frame, some think the narrator gently distances himself from the Teacher's more radical conclusions, and others think he endorses them, since he calls the Teacher wise and his words upright and true (12:9-10). Still others point out that the fear of God and God's judgment are not new ideas in the epilogue; the Teacher himself commanded the fear of God (5:7) and warned of judgment (3:17; 11:9). On this reading the conclusion does not overturn the Teacher's search but names where it was heading. The question of composition is open, but readers across these views agree that the book as it stands asks to be read with its conclusion.

questions: The Teacher urges the young to remember their Creator before old age comes. What would it mean for you to remember your Creator at your present stage of life?
The poem pictures aging and death with honesty and beauty. How does facing death directly, rather than avoiding it, change the way a person lives?
After all the Teacher's questions, the book concludes: fear God and keep his commandments. Does that conclusion satisfy you? Why or why not?
